Statement of Purpose
Ahmed Ali Hashmi — Graduate School of Data Science, KAIST
The ﬁrst time I watched a cursor move on a screen because someone simply thought about moving it, I
stopped thinking about brain-computer interfaces as a gimmick and started thinking about them as an
engineering problem with no clean solution. During my ﬁnal-year project, a BCI-controlled game driven by
EEG signals from a NeuroSky/OpenBCI headset, I ran into the issue that quietly derails most EEG work: a

model trained on one session, or one person, degrades sharply the moment the headset shifts half a
centimeter or the user's attention drifts. That gap between a model that works in the lab and one that works
for a real, distracted, physically different user is what pulled me toward my current research question — how
do we build learning systems that stay reliable and keep adapting when the data they see keeps changing
under them?

under them?
My background gave me the tools to chase that question properly rather than just intuitively. I'm completing
a BS in Computer Science at FAST-NUCES, Peshawar, with coursework spanning algorithms, probability and
statistics, numerical computing, and machine learning, alongside a semester in Harvard's Aspire Leaders
Program that pushed me to think about technology decisions in terms of long-term consequences, not just

short-term wins. The BCI project is where this training actually got tested: I preprocessed raw EEG with MNE
and SciPy, trained models to map concentration and relaxation states onto in-game actions, and had to
accept that the biggest bottleneck wasn't model capacity but non-stationarity in the signal itself — a
manuscript on this work is currently being prepared for submission. In parallel, I worked as a Data Scraping

Intern at Programming Force, where I built pipelines that had to keep functioning as source websites changed
structure without warning, an early, less glamorous lesson in the same theme of designing for drift rather
than assuming stability. More recently, as a Junior Network Engineer at Valyrian Systems, I analyze VPN
trafﬁc in Wireshark to detect patterns in encrypted payloads, which has sharpened my sense of how much

can be inferred, and how much can be missed, from imperfect, adversarial, real-world data streams. Together
these experiences moved me from "can I build this" to "can I trust what this builds."
That is the problem I want to spend my graduate work on: trustworthy and adaptive machine learning under
distribution shift, with biosignal and streaming data as the setting where the stakes are concrete rather than

abstract. If a BCI system meant to give a person with limited mobility control over a device silently fails when
their signal drifts, that's not a benchmark drop, it's a broken promise to the user. The same failure mode
shows up in federated and edge settings, where data is inherently non-IID across clients and devices. I want
to work on methods that can detect when they are operating outside their training distribution, adapt

without needing to be retrained from scratch, and do so in a way that a practitioner can actually verify and
trust.
This is why KAIST's Graduate School of Data Science is the right place for this work, and why I'm speciﬁcally
drawn to Professor Se-Young Yun's OSI Lab. His group's work on robust and communication-efﬁcient
federated learning, and on training methods that hold up under heterogeneous, shifting data, is directly

aligned with the adaptive-and-trustworthy framing I want to pursue, and I would welcome the chance to bring
my EEG and signal-processing background into that line of research. I'm also interested in Professor Jaegul
Choo's work on data-efﬁcient and generalizable representation learning, which speaks to the same core
problem from a different angle. GSDS's structure, with its emphasis on rigorous methodology alongside

applied, high-impact projects, is exactly the environment I need to turn a project-level intuition into a
properly formalized research contribution.
In my ﬁrst year, I plan to strengthen my theoretical foundation through GSDS coursework in statistical
learning and distributed systems while joining lab projects on robustness and domain adaptation, using my
BCI dataset as an early testbed for out-of-distribution detection methods. My thesis direction would extend

this toward adaptive learning algorithms for non-stationary, multi-user biosignal and edge-device data, with
an eye toward federated settings where data cannot be centralized. After graduation, I intend to pursue a
PhD or move into industrial R&D building reliable AI systems for healthcare and assistive technology, ideally
continuing to work between Pakistan and Korea's research ecosystems. My goal is straightforward: to help

make adaptive AI systems trustworthy enough that the people who depend on them most, including the
person I watched move a cursor with nothing but focus, never have to wonder whether the system will still
work tomorrow.

Set Up a Simple Gradio Interface to
Interact with Your Models
Estimated time: 30 minutes
Imagine you're developing a customer support chatbot for a company. The goal is to
provide a seamless and interactive way for customers to get answers to their
questions. To achieve this goal, you need an interface where users can input their
queries and receive responses generated by a large language model (LLM). This lab
guides you through the creation of such an interface using Gradio. You'll learn how to

integrate various Gradio components, including text input fields, buttons, and display
elements, to create an intuitive and user-friendly customer support experience.
Creating an interface is crucial for several reasons:
User accessibility: A front-end interface makes it easy for users to interact with
the LLM without needing technical expertise.
Enhanced user experience: An intuitive interface can provide a better user
experience, making interactions smoother and more efficient.

Customization: Gradio allows you to customize the interface to meet specific
needs, whether for a chatbot, a data analysis tool, or other applications.
Seamless integration: Gradio's flexibility enables you to seamlessly integrate the
front-end with various backend technologies, including LLMs.

Gradio Interface Inputs and Outputs
Common Inputs
Gradio has a large number of input types. The more commonly encountered ones are
listed below:
Checkbox : A checkbox that can be set to True  or False .
CheckboxGroup : An input type that allows users to select multiple values from a
predefined checkbox list.
Dropdown : An input type that provides a dropdown list where, by default, one
value can be selected. If multiselect  is set to True , then one or more values
can be selected.

can be selected.
File : An input type that allows a user to upload a file.
Image : An input type that allows the user to select or upload an image.
Radio : An input type that forces the user to choose one value.
Slider : An input type that provides a slider where a value must be selected
between a minimum and a maximum range. The value  parameter defines the
default value, and step  provides the increment value. Setting the minimum,

maximum, and step  values to integers will select integer values.
Textbox : An expandible text box that allows the user to type in text.
Common Outputs
Many of Gradio's input types can also function as outputs. The available output types
depend on the output of the function provided to Interface . In practice, for most
LLM applications, the output type is typically text. As such, a suitable choice is either
gr.Textbox() , or just "text" , which offers an expandable text box.The content of this lab is licensed underApache 2.0

Another frequently encountered output type is Label . Label  is typically used for
classification tasks, and can output the predicted probabilities of each class. If you
have a large number of classes, you can use the num_top_classes  parameter to
control the number of classes that are outputted. For instance, if you have 1000
classes, setting Label(num_top_classes=3)  would output just the three classes with

the highest predicted probabilities instead of the predicted probabilities for all classes.

IBM watsonx.ai LLM quickstart
watsonx.ai introduction
Watsonx.ai is IBM's commercial generative AI and scientific data platform based on
cloud technology that includes a studio, data store, and governance toolkit designed to
support multiple LLMs. This platform is designed to support a diverse array of AI
development tasks, providing developers with access to IBM's Granite models, Meta's
Llama models, Mistral AI's Mixtral model, and various others.

In this section, you will learn how to use watsonx.ai's API to create a simple Q&A bot.
This bot will leverage the advanced capabilities of watsonx.ai to understand and
respond to user queries accurately. Whether you're new to programming or an
experienced developer, this step-by-step tutorial will equip you with the knowledge to
integrate watsonx.ai's LLMs into your applications.

integrated into IBM's watsonx.ai platform, simplifying your development journey. The
provided API eliminates the need for generating complex API tokens, streamlining your
application creation process. The Llama and Mixtral models both support the following
use cases:
